sections.text: Thou must look at thy duty. Nothing can be more welcome to a soldier than a righteous war. Therefore to waver in this resolve is unworthy, O Arjuna!
Blessed are the soldiers who find their opportunity. This opportunity has opened for thee the gates of heaven.
अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि।
Refuse to fight in this righteous cause, and thou wilt be a traitor, lost to fame, incurring only sin.

We had been discussing Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge. So far we have seen in the chapter that Bhagavan explained to Arjuna his situation from various perspectives, not just one perspective, that this is my idea, you should do this. But he gave him various perspectives. The first perspective, spiritual perspective, from the highest perspective, from the spirits point of view that the self is immutable, imperishable. So thats the highest perspective. Then it came down to the societys perspective.
And see, from a societys perspective, you as a Kshatriya has duty to protect the society from evil. If you see that evil is occurring in the society, we rely on the Kshatriya just like we rely on our armies to protect ourselves. Our army cannot become pacifist at the last minute. From that perspective, this is the best opportunity you have to perform your art and perform your duty. So societys perspective, he gave his opinion that this is still what you should be looking at. Then came down the individuals perspective.
There we have seen Bhagavan said, if you give up, you run away from your duty, then you will incur sin. He has looked at the issue from various perspectives and came to the same conclusion that Arjuna should fight this war. So in the process, Bhagavan also taught us the art of persuasion. To persuade somebody who is bent upon doing something other than what we think is right for him, just giving your opinion that look, you are doing something wrong is not going to work. The only way that works is when you give him a three dimensional view of his situation, give him the view from various perspectives, look at it from various points of view and then the person will be able to see it correctly, then you will be able to persuade him. This can also be applied to looking at any problem or situation.
Say you come across a situation where you got a job in another town -- thats best for you. From your professional perspective, well, thats great. But if you take the decision just based on that, it may or may not be right. So you have to look at it from various perspectives. First you say, well from a professional perspective it seems like that job will give me more opportunity to go further in my career. Then you see it from familys perspective.
Will my family be comfortable relocating from this town to another? Will they be able to adjust as easily as they are adjusted here? Then lastly, you also have to see what the school district is in that new town. Is it as good or better in that town? And if you come to the same conclusion from all three of them, then relocation is the great idea. Take the job and move or you will find that you will end up commuting just like most of our friends do who work outside Richmond in Washington or or other places.
So any problem or situation cannot be viewed from just one perspective. And you can come to right decision or you can convince someone. So this art of persuasion is to give somebody a three dimensional view of a situation and then come to the conclusion. In this case, Bhagavan came to the same conclusion from all perspectives. From a spiritual, from a societys perspective, from individual Arjuna must fight this war. What typically works best is when it comes to me, I can see from my perspective that it is right.
So therefore Bhagavan put more stress on his individual situation. So we have seen that hes saying tathaha swadharma kirtim hitva papa vapsyasi. If you give up your duties, you will incur Papa. And this obviously is very dreaded word in Hindu society that you will incur papa. So that obviously worked probably more effectively. But you had the background of other two perspectives that this is right, this is the right thing to do from all perspectives.
So Bhagavan pursue that point of view a little further and says, bhayat ranat uparatam mansante tvam maharathaha isam chatvam bahumatah bhatva yasyasi lagavam. So all these great warriors who are gathered here on our side and on the other side, they have very high regards for you. Because of your valor and your prowess. Even your enemies are unwillingly accepting that you are one of the best warriors. It is not easy to confront you. You are the one who has achieved the pasupatastra from Lord Shiva himself.
Obviously theres a story that Arjunaya goes for tapas to please Lord Shiva. And in the end he ended up fighting with Lord Shiva himself. But Lord Shiva was so pleased that he revealed himself that I am not just the hunter which you are fighting, but I am Lord Shiva. Here is the Pashupadashtra. And as the Purana says, the Pasupatastra is like ultimate weapon. It can destroy the entire universe in no time.
So you are the one who has such a prowess that you can destroy everybody in no time if you really choose to. However, you cannot use any weapon irresponsibly. Just like our nuclear weapons. You may have capability but you may never use it. He said those people, they will then think that you ran away from this war because of fear. Even though that may not be reality but thats how you will be viewed by your peers and your enemies.
They will belittle you, they have high respect for you. And they will say I dont know what we were thinking. This guy turned out to be not really what we thought he is going to be. Its not something very comfortable for you if that happens. So the next verse says: not only will you disappoint your friends, relatives, and the people who are relying on you in society, but there are also Ahita people -- those who are not your well-wishers, your enemies who wish you would go away. They will be telling stories about your cowardice. All kinds of Bahun Avachya Vadaan -- things which we cannot repeat on national TV. That kind of talk, they will be talking about you. So please think about it.
Ninantaha, tava, samaratyam. They will be cavilling at your prowess. That I think it was all big hype. It was all made up stories that he is such a great warrior. I dont think he had those qualities. And if thats happened, what is more painful than that?
That nobody will ever realize that you ran away because you thought that killing your cousins and your teachers is not a right thing to do. But they will think its a fear of war, fear of defeat which made you go away. So dont think this is going to be easy. If you go away -- well, in any deal we make, you have to come up with a win-win situation. The only way the deal gets closed is when a client thinks I can provide the most appropriate services and I think this is the right project for me -- then only do we sign a contract. If either party doesnt think its right, nothing happens.
You have to come up with a win-win situation where both parties will have a good outcome. Now in this case, looking at our own situation, any decision I take from the options available to me -- I should feel comfortable that it will be an acceptable situation for me. So Bhagavan now uses that final trump card and says if you die, you will go to the heros heaven. So there is a special section of heaven which is reserved for these great heroes who die on the battlefield.
Its like the GI Bill, these great privileges in heaven for the heroes who serve their country, serve the society, in the process they die. You can think about the health care workers who lost their lives in this battle against Corona. So our scripture says there is a special section in heaven to reward them for their valor and their courage. Hatova Prapsesi Swargam Jitwava Bakshishe Mahim. If you die, you go to the heaven for the heroes. If you win, you will lead the kingdom on this earth.
This is a no-brainer for you. There is no way you can lose -- fight and die, or fight and win. Either way, you come out ahead. So there is nothing to think about. Here the only good decision is fight the war. Therefore he says, Tasmat Utthishtka Yudhaya Krutan Nishayah.
Therefore O son of Kunti, get up with a resolve to fight this war. So this is like a conclusive statement from Bhagavan. In the beginning Arjuna asked him and said, give me which is shreyas for me. And we have come across the word shreyas and prayers before. That which is always good. It may not feel good, but it is good for me.
Preyas feels good but is not good for me. And Arjuna, in no uncertain terms, asked Bhagavan: tell me what is good for me and I will do it. Now Bhagavan says Utthiste Kamanteya, get up with the resolve to fight this war. So that was the conclusive advice from Bhagavan. And then Bhagavan now introduces the concept of Karma Yoga. You have to act in this world and there will be consequences of your actions.
You are part of this world. This Sansa and this Sansar is not homogeneous experiences. The experiences are varied. Some are conducive, some are not conducive. You will fight the war. Outcome is not guaranteed.
The experience will not be as you predict. It may be something different. But you have to treat whatever you face with an equal state of mind. You have to treat them alike no matter what the outcome is. Because you are enjoying the ride in this world. The next verse now introduces the idea of how to transform Karma into Karma Yoga.
Same action, but changing the mental attitude, becomes Karma Yoga. It says: Sukha Dukhe Same Kritva Labha Alabhou Jaya Ajayou, Tato Yuddhaya Yujyasva, Naivam Papam Avapsyasi. We came back to Papa again. In verse 33 he said Tatah Svadharmam Kirtim Cha Hitva Papam Avapsyasi -- You will incur sin if you abandon your duty. Here he says Tatha yudhaya yujyashwa na evam papam avapshasi.
You will not incur any sin. But the condition is Sukha Dukhe Same Kritva -- you should treat pleasure and pain alike. Its more like being an observer. It does not mean that you react to pleasure and pain in the same way, but you treat them alike as an observer, maintaining equanimity.
For example, when someone thinks I should have a cup of coffee, the one who is thinking about having that cup of coffee -- thats an observer. That observer should be neutral, treating anything which comes with equanimity. Sukha and Dukha operate at the mental level -- these are my experiences. When I experience something, there will be a mental reaction saying this is conducive or this is not conducive, not good.
Then theres profit and loss, which operates at the intellectual level. Am I making profit by doing this or Im losing something? Here is my intellect. I actually thought Im gonna get this but I didnt get that.
And therefore this is a loss or this is a profit. So thats at the intellectual level. Finally both Jaya and Ajaya victory or defeat is at the physical level. I tried to gain something, I did not gain it. I competed against several firms to get a project. Thats a real reality, the physical reality that I dont have that project anymore.

Having established the spiritual foundation, Krishna now addresses Arjuna from the perspective of Dharma - righteous duty. Thou must look at thy duty. Nothing can be more welcome to a soldier than a righteous war. Therefore to waver in this resolve is unworthy (verse 31). This is Swadharma - ones own duty based on ones nature, training, and role in life. Arjuna is a Kshatriya, a warrior; protecting society from adharma is his sacred responsibility.
Verse 32 presents the opportunity positively: Blessed are the soldiers who find their opportunity. This opportunity has opened for thee the gates of heaven. Far from being a curse, facing this battle is actually a blessing - a chance to fulfill ones highest duty. But verse 33 warns of the consequences of abandoning that duty: Refuse to fight in this righteous cause, and thou wilt be a traitor, lost to fame, incurring only sin.
Apply this teaching by identifying your own Swadharma. What is your unique role, given your nature, skills, training, and circumstances? Are you fulfilling it, or are you wavering at a critical moment? Remember that Dharma is contextual - what is right changes based on time, place, and role. A soldiers dharma differs from a monks. Today, ask yourself: What is the righteous battle I am being called to fight? Where am I being asked to step up but holding back due to fear or attachment? What opportunity for growth or service am I treating as a burden rather than a blessing?
